column4: The section sets the hot spring against a flowing one; 55:44 places the deniers between the Fire and حَمِيمٍ آنٍ, making the spring itself part of punishment.
The section identifies the flowing spring with those who fear their Lord; 55:46 names those who fear their Lord's station and promises them two gardens, supplying the garden context for 55:50.
The section's ج ر ي note means water flowing; this ayah gives the God-fearing عَيْنَانِ تَجْرِيَانِ, the paired, moving counterpart to 55:44's boiling water.
The section distinguishes a running spring from a spring at the heat's limit; a second garden pair in 55 has عَيْنَانِ نَضَّاخَتَانِ, another explicit pair of active springs.
The section joins cups to the garden spring; 56:18 puts أكواب and أباريق beside a cup from مَعِين, joining serving vessels to visible flowing water.
The section says its root note for آنيَة gives a plural meaning vessels, unlike 88:5's hot-water adjective; 76:15 places آنية and أكواب together as the righteous are served.
The section links cups to ready garden provision; 76:16 continues 76:15 by specifying the crystal-like silver vessels and measured cups, completing that serving scene.
The section's garden spring is available to drink from; 76:6 describes a spring from which God's servants drink and make it gush forth as they will.
The section notes that the garden people are given a drink; 76:17 uses يُسْقَوْنَ for a cup blended with ginger, a specific counterpart to the punished drink.
The section contrasts a flowing garden spring with the hot spring; 76:18 names Salsabil as a spring in that same garden drink scene.
The section contrasts the hot spring with provision in the garden; 76:21 says their Lord gives them a purifying drink, making the giver and the drink's quality explicit.
The section notes يُسْقَوْنَ for a sealed pure drink; 83:25 gives the righteous that drink, reversing the punished people’s hot spring.
The section cites the sealed drink in 83:25; 83:26 continues its description by saying its seal is musk, adding a concrete detail to that garden beverage.
The section connects garden drinking to its source; 83:27 says the drink is blended with Tasnim, explaining its composition before 83:28 identifies the spring.
The section contrasts the two springs; 83:28 names a spring from which those brought near drink, a direct garden counterpart to 88:5.
The section asks who could restore water if it sinks away; 67:30 asks who will bring مَاءٍ مَّعِينٍ if their water becomes غَوْرًا, making dependence on a visible source explicit.
The section contrasts an available flowing spring with water that may disappear; 23:18 says water is settled in the earth and that God can take it away.
The section asks who could bring water if it sinks; 18:41 applies that danger to a garden's water, saying it may become sunken beyond recovery.
The section treats drinking water as provision whose source is not human; 56:68 asks people to consider the water they drink, beginning the question of who supplies it.
The section asks who brings the spring water; 56:69 asks whether people or God sent down their drinking water from the clouds, naming its source.
The section's root note ع ذ ب distinguishes sweet water from punishment; 56:70 says God could make drinking water أُجَاجًا, a bitter reversal of sweet water.

The section explicitly names عَذْبٌ as its dictionary form for sweet water, set against عَذَاب punishment; 25:53 calls one sea عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ and the other bitter, making the water-quality distinction concrete.
The section's dictionary form عَذْبٌ means pleasant water, while 88:24 uses the cognate for punishment; 35:12 contrasts عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ water with salty, bitter water.
The section contrasts sweet water with a hot spring; 77:27 says God gave people مَاءً فُرَاتًا, making pleasant drinking water the reverse of the punishment drink.
The section pairs food that fails to relieve hunger with hot water; 69:36 says the condemned have no food except غِسْلِين, a close parallel to the exclusive, non-nourishing food in 88:6–7.
The section describes a food allotted to the condemned; 69:37 completes 69:36 by specifying that only the sinners eat it.
The section makes the punishment meal a combination of drink and food; 73:13 names choking food and painful punishment, another scene where eating itself is part of torment.
The section says the condemned remain hungry; 20:118 describes the garden where Adam will neither go hungry nor unclothed, a direct boundary against deprivation.
The section makes thirst meet boiling water; 20:119 says Adam will not thirst or suffer the sun's heat in the garden, reversing thirst and scorching.
The section contrasts punished thirst with a garden spring; 7:50 has the Fire's people beg the Garden's people to pour water on them, but they are refused.
The section's hot spring is a drink of punishment; 18:29 says the wrongdoers receive water like molten metal that scalds their faces, turning water into torment.
The section contrasts a garden's drink with punitive water; 14:16 says the condemned are given water of صَدِيد, a foul drink instead of a nourishing spring.
The section describes water that cannot satisfy; 14:17 continues the painful drink of 14:16, saying the person struggles to swallow it and death comes from every side.
The section's hot spring is punishment served as water; 22:19 says boiling water is poured over the heads of the disbelievers, making the drink an imposed torment.
The section makes the hot drink bodily punishment; 22:20 completes 22:19 by saying it melts what is in their bellies and their skins.
The section contrasts flowing water with a boiling source; 40:72 says the condemned are in boiling water and then fueled in the Fire.
The section opposes the hot spring to refreshing garden water; 78:24 says the people of Hell taste neither coolness nor drink.
The section names a spring at the limit of heat; 78:25 specifies that the Hell dwellers receive only boiling water and ghassaq.
The section pairs punitive drink with food; 56:52 identifies the food of the deniers as fruit from the tree of Zaqqum, which the next verses make them eat and drink alongside.
The section says the punished food does not satisfy hunger; 56:53 says the deniers fill their bellies from Zaqqum, setting up the drink that follows.
The section's hot spring is an imposed drink; 56:54 says the deniers drink boiling water over the Zaqqum, directly joining the two sides of the punishment meal.
The section contrasts running water with a drink that cannot quench; 56:55 likens the deniers' drinking to thirsty camels.
The section pairs food with hot water and says it cannot relieve hunger; 37:66 says the deniers eat from Zaqqum until their bellies are full.
The section contrasts the garden spring with a punitive drink; 37:67 says a mixture of boiling water follows the Zaqqum meal.
The section describes an imposed, harmful food and drink; 44:44 identifies Zaqqum as the food of the sinner.
The section makes eating part of punishment; 44:45 says the food boils in the bellies like molten dregs.
The section's عين آنية is a spring whose heat has reached its limit; 44:46 compares the boiling in the belly to the boiling of حَمِيم.
The section joins boiling water to عَذَاب punishment; 44:48 commands that boiling water from عَذَابِ الْحَمِيم be poured over the sinner's head.
The section contrasts flowing spring water with a punitive drink; 38:57 makes the wrongdoers taste boiling water and ghassaq.
The section's garden spring is part of provision; 38:51 shows the garden's people reclining and calling for abundant fruit and drink.
The section says the garden spring is renewed while hot water is fixed punishment; 38:54 says the garden provision does not run out.
The section contrasts hot water with a renewed garden spring; 47:15 describes rivers of water that does not change, then the condemned being given boiling water.
The section sets hot water as punishment against a flowing garden spring; 10:4 says the disbelievers receive a drink of boiling water and painful punishment, a direct parallel to that punitive drink.
The section connects drinking to a spring; 37:45 has a cup from مَعِين passed among the righteous, joining the cup to its source.
The section contrasts the hot spring with garden drink; 37:46 describes the drink in the cup of 37:45 as white and delightful to drinkers.
The section contrasts punishment drink with garden provision; 37:47 completes the description of the cup in 37:45 by saying it causes no harm or loss of sense.
The section sets hunger and boiling water against garden provision; 52:19 tells the people of the Garden to eat and drink in satisfaction.
The section describes cups set ready in the garden; 52:23 has the garden's people pass a cup among themselves, a moving form of the same cup scene.
The section places cups among garden furnishings; 52:24 continues the cup scene with youths circulating among the garden's people in service.
The section connects cups with the garden; 43:71 shows golden dishes and أكواب being served there, with what the souls desire and eyes delight in.
The section's cups are placed ready in the garden; 78:34 describes a garden cup as كَأْسًا دِهَاقًا, an overflowing cup rather than a punitive drink.
The section says cups are already at hand; 69:23 says the Garden's fruit clusters hang near, a parallel of provision made accessible.
The section pairs hunger with a drink that cannot satisfy; 69:24 tells the righteous to eat and drink in satisfaction, reversing that punishment.
The section says the cups are placed within reach; 76:14 continues the garden scene by saying its fruit clusters are made easy to reach.
The section contrasts the hot spring with moving, replenishing water; 56:31 describes the people of the right receiving water poured out for them.
The section presents food and drink as garden provision; 56:32 adds abundant fruit to the garden scene around the poured water.
The section says the running spring renews; 56:33 says the garden fruit is neither cut off nor forbidden, a parallel of provision that remains available.
The section places a flowing spring in the garden of the God-fearing; 77:41 gives the God-fearing shade and springs after the passage on Hell's punishment.
The section contrasts unrelieved hunger and hot water with garden provision; 77:43 tells the righteous to eat and drink in satisfaction for what they did.
The section places its flowing spring among garden furnishings; 15:45 says the God-fearing are in gardens and springs, the same reward setting.
The section associates a spring with the garden of the God-fearing; 51:15 repeats that they are in gardens and springs.
The section sets the punished boiling spring against garden water; 44:52 says the God-fearing are in gardens and springs after the passage on Zaqqum and boiling water.
The section presents springs as provision in a garden; 26:134 describes the worldly abundance of ʿĀd as gardens and springs, linking the spring image to provision.
The section joins a spring with food and garden life; 26:147 describes gardens, springs, crops, and date palms in the provision promised to Thamud.
The section asks what happens when water is withdrawn; 26:57 describes Pharaoh's people being made to leave gardens and springs, a scene of lost abundance.
The section asks who could restore a spring if it sank; 44:25 says Pharaoh's people left gardens and springs behind, marking the loss of water and provision.
The section describes drinks given to the people of the Garden; 76:5 says the righteous drink a cup blended with camphor, another specific garden beverage.

The section's ط ع م note treats eating as nourishment and includes water; 76:8 uses the food root for feeding the needy, orphan, and captive, a concrete act that relieves hunger rather than imposing it.
The section's food fails to relieve hunger; 90:14 praises feeding during a day of severe hunger, a specific reversal of that deprivation.

The section contrasts two named springs by what their water does; 2:60 describes Moses striking a rock so twelve springs gush out and each group knows where to drink, a concrete communal spring scene.
The section treats the flowing spring as provision; 7:160 repeats the spring-gushing scene and explicitly tells the people to eat and drink from God's provision.

The section stresses that springs share a name while their qualities differ; 13:4 says gardens are watered by one water yet differ in their produce, a specific parallel between common source and unlike outcomes.
The section places moving water in a garden; 18:33 describes two gardens through which a river runs, a concrete garden-and-flowing-water parallel.
The section joins water to food as provision; 23:19 continues the account of water settled in the earth in 23:18 by describing gardens, abundant fruit, and eating from it.
The section's garden has a flowing spring; 36:34 says God made gardens and caused springs to gush in them, a direct garden-and-spring scene.
The section treats drinking and food as one provision; 36:35 completes the garden-and-spring scene of 36:34 by saying people may eat from its fruit.
The section contrasts moving spring water with water that may sink away; 39:21 describes rain made into springs in the earth, then plants drying and crumbling, showing the source's renewal and loss.
The section links garden springs with nourishment; 55:67 continues the pair of gushing springs in 55:66 by naming the date palms and pomegranates of those gardens.
The section says placed cups are the opposite of raised furnishings; 56:34 describes raised couches in the garden scene whose preceding verses mention poured water and enduring fruit.
The section makes the hot spring a punishment drink; 56:42 places the condemned in scorching wind and boiling water, repeating the punitive heat-and-water pairing.
The section opposes the hot spring to refreshing garden water; 56:44 says the punishment's shade is neither cool nor beneficial, clarifying that no relief comes from the scene.
The section sets garden drink against punitive food and water; 37:62 asks whether the garden's welcome or the tree of Zaqqum is the better provision, introducing the contrast that 37:66–67 completes.
